newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA TO SEAL NUCLEAR DEALS IN JANUARY.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA TO SEAL NUCLEAR DEALS IN JANUARY.

text.p: Bulgaria plans to seal deals on modernising its two largest nuclear reactors at Kozloduy and on building a storage facility for highly radioactive spent fuel in January, Energy Minister Roumen Ovcharov said on Saturday.

The energy ministry issued two tenders earlier this year for the modernisation of its two more modern 1,000-megawatt reactors and to plan technological specifications for a new spent fuel storage facility.
"We will announce the winners of the two tenders in January next year," Ovcharov told Reuters.
Tender conditions for a $250 million reconstruction of the two reactors included helping Bulgaria receive loans from international financial institutions to fund the modernisation.
Kozloduy's reactor number five has been in operation since 1987, while number six was licensed in December 1993 after a two-year commissioning period.
A consortium of Germany's Siemens AG , France's Framatome and a Russian institute is among the bidders.
U.S.-based Westinghouse Electric Corp has also unveiled a modernisation programme and financial proposals.
Bids from three firms are being considered for a technological project to plan the dry waste storage facility, which will hold spent fuel for up to 50 years.
In the past, the Soviet Union reprocessed and disposed of spent fuel from all the six reactors at Kozloduy without charge under a bilateral agreement which expired in 1990.

The spent fuel has since been left unprocessed in a temporary storage at Kozloduy. Moscow adopted a law on environmental protection in 1992 which banned the shipment of nuclear waste to its territory.

Ovcharov said last week ministry experts, who visited Russia, had settled problems with transportation of nuclear fuel via Moldova and Ukraine. Earlier this year Romania approved fuel transportation through its Danube river waters.

"We have practically agreed the transportation of fresh nuclear fuel with Russia, Ukraine and Moldova and by February we expect to sign a government agreement with these countries," Ovcharov told reporters.

With the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Bulgaria needs special permission from Ukraine and Moldova to transport Russian nuclear fuel supplies through their territory. Kozloduy meets more than 40 percent of Bulgaria's fuel needs.
